name: Italian irredentism
summary: Italian irredentism was a late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century movement in the Kingdom of Italy and in Austrian-ruled Trento and Trieste that demanded the annexation of the 'unredeemed lands' (Trentino, Trieste, and by extension Istria, Fiume and parts of Dalmatia) inhabited mainly by Italian speakers, to complete national unification. It was an opinion movement rather than a doctrine of government, so its sources say little beyond the national question, and it largely ended when Trento and Trieste were annexed after 1918.

scope: The late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Italian movement for annexing the Italian-inhabited lands outside the Kingdom of Italy, mainly Trentino and Trieste, as the defining sources (the Columbia Encyclopedia and Stibbe's 1914-1918-online entry) describe it, with Cesare Battisti's 1914-15 lectures as the movement's own statement of the case. It excludes the Fascist expansion of the claims to Corsica, Malta, Nice, Savoy and Dalmatia, which Stibbe treats as a later nationalist use, and it leaves out Battisti's socialist views, which his lectures present as his own and not as part of the irredentist cause.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The movement's defining aim was the annexation to Italy of lands outside its borders inhabited by an Italian majority (Trentino, Trieste, Istria, Fiume, parts of Dalmatia), as the Columbia Encyclopedia and Stibbe define it; Battisti's lectures argue the same claim for the Trentino and Trieste.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Battisti defines a state as the union of those who share a language and a common historical consciousness, and condemns Austria as a conglomerate of ten nations; the defining accounts present the movement as seeking states matching Italian-speaking populations.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Battisti's lecture honours the dead of the Risorgimento and the irredentist exiles as heroes whose sacrifice is to be commemorated, and Stibbe records Battisti's execution by Austria as a turning point for the cause.

national-self-determination.rationale: Battisti's lectures argue that Italy's liberation of its irredent lands would also let Poles, Romanians and South Slavs form their own united states, and name the Mazzinian federation of nation-states as the aim.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Battisti's lectures denounce Austrian suppression of Italian schools and the Italian language in the irredent lands as the destruction of the stock's character, and the movement's defence of Italian language and culture is described in the sources as central.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Battisti's lecture 'Trento, Trieste e il dovere d'Italia' presents the Kingdom of Italy's duty to its Italian brothers under Austrian rule as the core of the cause, and the encyclopedia accounts describe the movement as agitating in Italy itself for their liberation.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Irredentists held that the Italian nation was left incomplete when parts stayed under Austrian rule after the wars of independence, and demanded their union with the Kingdom of Italy; Battisti calls the failure to finish unification a stain to be erased.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Irredentists campaigned for Italy to leave neutrality and join the Entente against Austria-Hungary, the 1915 Treaty of London bringing Italy in; Battisti scorns the hope that neutrality will win the lands.

missingStatements.text: A country should go to war to bring land inhabited by its own nationals under foreign rule into its borders.
missingStatements.rationale: Battisti rejects relying on diplomacy to win Trento and Trieste, and Stibbe records pro-interventionist groups mobilising the unredeemed territories for Italy's entry into war in 1915.

quotes.text: Il ritenere che pei begli occhi della neutralità italiana, le nazioni belligeranti debbano donare all’Italia le terre irredente non è cosa da pazzi, ma da delinquenti.

notes: Themes searched: territorial claims, language and culture, war and neutrality, alliances, democracy and rights under Austrian rule, economy, religion, colonialism, minorities. The defining sources (an encyclopedia definition, an Italian encyclopedia entry, a scholarly overview and a Trentino leader's lectures) concern the national question; the movement had no programme on economy, government, religion, society or ecology, so those statements are null. The Fascist-era extension of the claims is not the ideology's, per Stibbe. Battisti's socialism and his European federation hope are his own views and were not used.
